meta.title: Lab-Grown Diamonds vs Moissanite
meta.description: Compare lab-grown diamonds and moissanite by material, sparkle, hardness, price and everyday wear to choose the right stone for you.

heroIntro.title: Lab-Grown Diamonds vs Moissanite:
heroIntro.subtitle: What Is the Difference?
paragraphs: Laboratory-grown diamonds and moissanite are durable, sparkling stones used in modern jewellery, but they are not the same material.

A laboratory-grown diamond is diamond material created using a controlled technological process. It consists of crystallised carbon and has essentially the same chemical, physical and optical properties as a natural diamond. Moissanite is silicon carbide. The moissanite used in jewellery is manufactured because naturally occurring moissanite is exceptionally rare.

The most visible difference is often their light performance. Diamond produces a balance of brightness, fire and scintillation. Moissanite has greater dispersion and frequently displays stronger rainbow-coloured flashes. Some people prefer diamond's familiar light pattern, while others deliberately choose moissanite for its more colourful fire.
Both can be suitable for everyday jewellery. Your choice should depend on whether owning diamond matters to you, the type of sparkle you prefer, the size you want and your budget.

items: Laboratory-grown diamond is diamond; moissanite is silicon carbide
Moissanite is a distinct gemstone and diamond simulant, not a type of diamond
Diamond scores 10 on the Mohs scale; moissanite about 9.25–9.5
Moissanite generally displays more rainbow-coloured fire
Moissanite usually costs less than a comparable lab-grown diamond
Both suit frequently worn earrings when properly set and cared for
Neither should be treated as a guaranteed financial investment

content.text: Laboratory-grown diamond is diamond material. Moissanite is a different gemstone that can be used as a diamond alternative.

Both are highly resistant to scratching and both can work in everyday jewellery. The practical differences are the type of sparkle, the price at a given visible size and whether owning diamond specifically matters to you.
What are lab-grown diamonds?

rows: Distinct manufactured gemstone and diamond simulant
Yes, when accurately described as laboratory-grown
Laboratory production of gem-quality silicon carbide
Doubly refractive, although cutting can minimise the visible effect
Lighter at the same visible dimensions
Buyers who prefer stronger fire or a lower price

content.text: The Mohs scale measures resistance to scratching. It is not a complete measure of toughness or indestructibility. Both stones can still be damaged by a sufficiently hard impact, and the metal or setting can fail even when the stone remains intact.
A laboratory-grown diamond is produced using technology that enables diamond crystal growth. The two principal production methods are:

items: High Pressure High Temperature: HPHT uses high pressure and temperature to produce diamond material.
Chemical Vapour Deposition: CVD introduces a carbon-rich gas into a controlled chamber and deposits carbon onto a diamond seed.

content.text: The resulting rough diamond is cut and polished for use in jewellery. Its laboratory origin should be disclosed clearly in the product title, description, receipt, packaging and accompanying documentation.
Laboratory-grown diamonds are not moissanite, cubic zirconia or another diamond simulant. They are diamond material with a different origin from natural diamonds.
Are lab-grown diamonds real diamonds?

Moissanite is silicon carbide. The natural mineral was identified in the late nineteenth century, but naturally occurring crystals are extremely rare and generally unsuitable for producing commercial quantities of jewellery.
The moissanite sold in modern jewellery is therefore manufactured. It is cut into gemstones that can be colourless or near-colourless and is available in numerous shapes and sizes.

Moissanite is often described as a diamond alternative because it is bright, durable and usually less expensive. However, it has its own composition and optical properties. Someone may choose moissanite because they genuinely prefer it—not merely because they cannot purchase diamond.
No. Moissanite is a legitimate gemstone when it is accurately disclosed and sold as moissanite.

It is not diamond, but a product does not become "fake" simply because it is made from a different material. Misrepresentation occurs when a seller describes moissanite as diamond or fails to disclose what the stone is.
The clearer description is that moissanite is a manufactured silicon-carbide gemstone that can be used as a diamond alternative.
The product title, specifications and receipt should use "moissanite", not vague descriptions such as "diamond-like stone" or "diamond alternative" without identifying the material.
No. Laboratory-grown diamonds are diamonds created through a technological process rather than geological formation.

Their laboratory origin remains an important difference and must be communicated clearly. Simply using the word "diamond" without a nearby laboratory-grown qualifier can cause shoppers to assume that the product contains natural diamonds.
Lab-grown vs natural diamonds
Moissanite has greater dispersion than diamond. Dispersion is the separation of white light into spectral colours, which creates rainbow-coloured flashes known as fire.
This means moissanite often produces more noticeable rainbow flashes, particularly:

items: As the stone or wearer moves

content.text: Diamond also produces fire, but its appearance is usually perceived as a different balance of white brightness, coloured fire and dark-to-light scintillation.
Neither appearance is objectively better. Choose based on preference:

rows: Either, depending on cut and quality
Highly visible sparkle at a lower price

content.text: Moissanite is not universally "too rainbow" or "artificial" looking. The visual effect depends on the cut, size, lighting and the wearer's preference.

content.heading: Which looks more like a natural diamond?

content.text: A laboratory-grown diamond looks like a natural diamond because both are diamond material and have essentially the same optical properties. Their different origins normally cannot be established through casual visual inspection.

Moissanite can resemble diamond, but it interacts with light differently. Some cuts may also show visible doubling of facet junctions because moissanite is doubly refractive. Modern cutting techniques can reduce this effect.

A photograph is not a reliable identification tool. Lighting, focus, stone size, camera exposure and editing can make two different materials look more similar—or more different—than they appear in person.

If the goal is specifically the appearance and material properties of diamond, choose laboratory-grown diamond. If the goal is a bright, durable stone with more colourful fire, moissanite may be preferable.

Both stones are highly durable for jewellery. Diamond scores 10 on the Mohs scale, giving it the highest scratch resistance of commonly used gemstones. Moissanite scores approximately 9.25–9.5, making it more resistant to scratching than most other jewellery stones.
However, scratch resistance is only one consideration. Both stones can potentially chip or become loose after an impact. Earrings also include components that may wear independently:
For earrings, the construction and care routine can be just as important as the stone itself.
Remove either type before swimming, showering, strenuous exercise and sleeping in delicate or long designs. Check settings periodically and stop wearing an earring if a stone moves.
Moissanite usually costs less than a laboratory-grown diamond of similar visible size.

However, comparing only carat figures can be misleading. Carat is a measure of weight, not diameter. Moissanite is less dense than diamond, so a moissanite and a diamond with the same visible dimensions do not weigh the same.

Moissanite sellers may use terms such as diamond-equivalent weight, DEW or diamond-equivalent carat weight. These figures estimate the weight of a diamond with similar dimensions. They are not the moissanite's actual weight. The product page should state the stone's dimensions in millimetres and explain whether a carat figure is actual or diamond-equivalent.
The final price also depends on:

content.heading: Do laboratory-grown diamonds hold more value than moissanite?

content.text: Laboratory-grown diamonds generally have a higher initial retail price than moissanite, but that does not guarantee higher resale value or future price retention.

Laboratory-grown diamond prices have changed substantially as manufacturing capacity and technology have developed. Moissanite also has an active retail market but should not be treated as a financial asset.
Purchase either stone primarily for its appearance, its wearability, its meaning, its design and the enjoyment it provides. Neither is an investment product.
Are lab-grown diamonds worth it?
Choose laboratory-grown diamond earrings when:

items: You want the product to be described and gifted as diamond jewellery.
You are building a collection around laboratory-grown diamonds.
Diamond material is part of the purchase's meaning.

content.text: Choose moissanite earrings when:

items: You want a larger visible size for a lower price.
Diamond identity is not important to you.
You want a durable gemstone alternative.
You already own and enjoy moissanite jewellery.

content.text: The right answer is not determined by any retailer's inventory. I Want Jewels specialises in laboratory-grown diamonds, but moissanite genuinely suits some shoppers better.
Stud earrings make the differences in size, weight and sparkle particularly relevant. Compare studs using:

items: Whether moissanite weight is expressed as DEW
The combined weight of both earrings

content.text: A product described as "one-carat moissanite studs" may refer to diamond-equivalent size rather than one carat of actual moissanite weight. The specification should make this clear.
Lab-grown diamond stud earrings guide
Lab-grown diamond earring size guide

content.heading: Which is better for everyday wear?

content.text: Both stones have sufficient scratch resistance for frequent wear. The better option depends more on the preferred appearance, the jewellery construction and whether owning diamond matters.
For everyday earrings, prioritise:

items: A finish compatible with your care routine

content.text: Moissanite's durability makes it a genuine everyday option, not merely an occasional substitute. Laboratory-grown diamond offers greater scratch resistance, but the complete earring still requires appropriate care.
Can you wear lab-grown diamond earrings every day?

content.heading: Which is better for a gift?

content.text: A gift is not automatically more meaningful because one material costs more.

Choose laboratory-grown diamond when the recipient has requested diamond, the occasion is specifically being marked with diamond jewellery, the buyer wants the gift described as laboratory-grown diamond, or diamond is part of the intended symbolism.

Choose moissanite when the recipient already wears moissanite, prefers stronger rainbow-coloured sparkle, prioritises size or design within a particular budget, or simply prefers alternative gemstones.
The stone must always be disclosed. The recipient should never be left to assume that moissanite is diamond, or that a laboratory-grown diamond is natural.
Lab-grown diamond earrings for gifts
Neither stone earns a blanket sustainability claim simply because it is produced in a laboratory.
Environmental impact can depend on:

A retailer should use claims such as "sustainable", "eco-friendly" or "carbon-neutral" only when it has current evidence supporting the specific product and supply chain. The same rule applies to ethical-sourcing claims. Laboratory production alone does not prove every environmental or social claim.

content.heading: Can a diamond tester distinguish them?

content.text: Not every diamond tester can reliably distinguish moissanite from diamond.

Moissanite has relatively high thermal conductivity, so some older or thermal-only diamond testers may register moissanite as diamond. Modern testers may combine thermal and electrical-conductivity measurements, but results still depend on the instrument, calibration and operator.
A positive result from a simple tester does not establish whether a stone is:
Use a qualified gemologist or professional gemological laboratory when reliable identification is necessary. Do not use scratch tests or other potentially destructive home methods.

content.heading: How do you clean laboratory-grown diamond and moissanite?

content.text: Both stones can collect skin oils, cosmetics, soap and hair-product residue. This buildup can reduce visible sparkle.

The cleaning method must account for the complete earring—not just the stone. A method that is safe for diamond or moissanite may not be suitable for gold plating, delicate settings or other decorative materials.
Follow the retailer's care instructions and avoid:
How to clean lab-grown diamond earrings

content.heading: What should you check before buying?

content.text: Before purchasing either stone, confirm the following.
Stone identity
The product should explicitly say "laboratory-grown diamond" or "moissanite".
Dimensions
Check the stone diameter in millimetres rather than relying only on carat terminology.
Weight terminology
Determine whether the stated weight is actual carat weight, total carat weight or diamond-equivalent weight.
Pair versus individual earring
For earrings, verify whether the listed weight applies to the complete pair or each earring.
Metal and finish
Check whether the jewellery uses solid gold, gold-plated sterling silver, unplated silver or another material.
Documentation
Ask what stone and product documentation is provided. Small stones used in earrings may not have individual laboratory reports, but the retailer should still provide accurate specifications.
Returns and aftercare
Review the returns policy, warranty, repairs and cleaning instructions.

content.heading: Laboratory-grown diamond or moissanite: the final decision

content.text: Choose laboratory-grown diamond if owning diamond matters to you and you prefer diamond's balance of brightness, fire and scintillation.
Choose moissanite if you prefer stronger rainbow-coloured fire, want a larger visible size for your budget or simply like moissanite as a gemstone.
Both can be durable and beautiful. The most important requirements are accurate disclosure, appropriate pricing and a well-made setting.
Lab-grown diamonds vs cubic zirconia

faq.question: Is moissanite a laboratory-grown diamond?
faq.answer: No. Moissanite is laboratory-manufactured silicon carbide. Laboratory-grown diamond is crystallised carbon.

faq.question: Is moissanite a real gemstone?
faq.answer: Yes. Moissanite is a recognised gemstone material. The moissanite used commercially is manufactured because naturally occurring material is extremely rare.

faq.question: Which is harder: moissanite or laboratory-grown diamond?
faq.answer: Diamond scores 10 on the Mohs scale. Moissanite is approximately 9.25–9.5. Both are highly resistant to scratching.

faq.question: Which has more sparkle?
faq.answer: Moissanite generally displays stronger rainbow-coloured fire. Diamond produces its own balance of brightness, fire and scintillation.

faq.question: Does moissanite become cloudy?
faq.answer: Moissanite does not normally become chemically cloudy, but oils, cosmetics, soap and residue can reduce visible sparkle. Appropriate cleaning may remove this buildup.

faq.question: Can you tell moissanite from diamond by looking?
faq.answer: Sometimes their optical differences are visible, particularly in larger stones, but visual inspection is not a reliable authentication method.

faq.question: Can moissanite pass a diamond tester?
faq.answer: Some thermal-only testers may register moissanite as diamond. Professional identification requires suitable equipment and expertise.

faq.question: Is moissanite cheaper than laboratory-grown diamond?
faq.answer: Generally, yes. Compare the complete piece and use millimetre dimensions because moissanite and diamond have different densities.

faq.question: Which is better for sensitive ears?
faq.answer: The stone does not usually determine skin compatibility. The post, base metal, plating, nickel content and individual sensitivity are more relevant.

cta.heading: Choose laboratory-grown diamond if owning diamond matters to you and you prefer its balance of brightness, fire and scintillation. Choose moissanite if you prefer stronger rainbow fire or a larger visible size for your budget.
